content.purpose: Recognise, before pressing Enter, which commands can destroy data.
content.mentalModel: Six commands do most of the damage. rm deletes with no recycle bin. sudo removes the safety net of permissions. chmod and chown change who can reach a file, and can lock you out of your own work or open it to everyone. kill stops a running program, possibly mid-write. shutdown stops the machine. What makes them dangerous is rarely the command itself: it is the argument. rm report.txt is fine; rm -rf / is not, and the difference is one wildcard or one stray space away.
syntax: rm FILE                  delete a file, permanently
rm -r DIRECTORY          delete a directory and everything in it
ls PATTERN               see what a wildcard matches before you act on it

demonstration.explanation: The habit worth building: run ls with the pattern first. The shell expands the wildcard before the command sees it, so this shows you the exact list rm would have deleted.

remember: rm has no recycle bin, and there is no undo
The shell expands wildcards before the command runs, so ls with the same pattern tells you what will be affected
sudo turns a permission error into a completed action, which is sometimes the only thing standing between you and a broken system
Take a snapshot before anything you are unsure about

commonOptions.meaning: Recurse into directories, which multiplies the consequences
Force: suppress questions and ignore missing files

dangerous: rm -rf with a wildcard or an absolute path
A space in the wrong place: rm -rf / home/student is not rm -rf /home/student
sudo in front of a command you have not read

tasks.instruction: The directory /home/student/audit contains a mixture of files. Some end in .tmp and are disposable; the rest must survive. Before deleting anything, list what the pattern *.tmp matches inside that directory and save that list to /home/student/audit-plan.txt.

validators.message: audit-plan.txt does not list the .tmp files. List what the pattern matches before deleting.
keep-me.txt has been deleted. The point of listing first is to avoid exactly this.

tasks.instruction: Now delete only the disposable files from /home/student/audit. Everything not ending in .tmp must still be there afterwards.

validators.message: The audit directory does not contain exactly the files that should have survived. Check that every .tmp file is gone and nothing else was removed.

tasks.instruction: Write a single line into /home/student/why-dangerous.txt naming the command from this lesson that deletes data with no way to recover it. The file must contain that command's name.

validators.message: why-dangerous.txt does not name the command. Which one deletes files permanently?

tasks.suggestedSolution: echo 'rm deletes permanently with no recycle bin' > /home/student/why-dangerous.txt

reviewQuestions.question: Which of these commands can destroy or lose data? Choose all that apply.
reviewQuestions.explanation: rm deletes, chown -R can make files unreachable to their owner, and kill -9 stops a program with no chance to save. ls and pwd only read.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does listing a wildcard before deleting with it help?
answers: The shell expands the wildcard before the command runs, so ls shows the exact same list rm would receive
ls locks the files so they cannot be deleted
rm ignores wildcards unless you list them first
It does not help; it is superstition
reviewQuestions.explanation: Wildcard expansion happens in the shell, not in the command, so any command given the same pattern receives the same list.
